key_terms.meaning: Media whose data has no time axis: text, image, still graphics. Display order is chosen by the user or the document, not fixed by the data itself.
Media whose meaning depends on when each piece is presented: audio, video, animation. A late sample is a wrong sample.
The measured time offset between two streams that should be aligned, e.g. audio and video; skew beyond about 80 ms is noticed by viewers.
Storage, processing and delivery spread over several machines that must still present one shared timeline to the user.
A short list of numbers describing media content (colour histogram, MFCC coefficients, motion energy) stored so that similarity can be computed as distance.
Answering a query by comparing feature vectors rather than by exact keyword match; ranked by distance, not by equality.
A shared vocabulary of concepts and their relations (person, vehicle, event, place) used to label media so different systems can query it the same way.
A stored connection from an anchor inside one media node to another node or to a position inside it; the link carries the destination and the conditions for following it.
Transport protocol that adds sequence numbers and timestamps to media packets so the receiver can rebuild timing and detect loss.
A set of measurable promises for a flow: bandwidth, delay, jitter and loss, each with a target value and units.
Variation in packet arrival delay, measured in milliseconds; playout buffers exist mainly to absorb it.
Delaying or pacing packets so a flow stays inside its promised rate; a token bucket of depth b bytes and rate r bytes/s is the standard model.
Refusing a new flow when its promised resources would push existing flows past their QoS targets; overload is prevented instead of repaired.
Cutting a stored media file into short, independently fetchable chunks (typically 2–10 s) so the client can choose what to fetch next.
Client measures throughput and buffer level, then picks the next segment from the highest bitrate version that the link can sustain.
Earliest-deadline-first: the runnable task with the nearest deadline runs next. It suits periodic media tasks, which must finish before each playout instant.
Ordered stages — capture, detect, describe, index, store — that turn raw camera or phone media into searchable records faster than a human could watch it.
A mark embedded in the media signal itself so that it survives compression, resizing or re-recording and can later prove ownership or origin.
Hiding data by replacing the lowest bit of each sample or pixel; invisible to the eye but destroyed by almost any processing.
Computing a compact perceptual hash of the content so that copies, even edited ones, map to the same identifier and can be matched against a database.

takeaways: A multimedia system is a pipeline of capture, compress, buffer, synchronise, store, deliver and present, and every stage is designed around the timing of temporal media.
Non-temporal media can be delivered late without harm; temporal media cannot, and that single fact explains buffering, QoS and real-time scheduling.
A distributed multimedia system adds network delay and clock differences to the problem, so one shared timeline must be reconstructed at the receiver.
Multimedia databases answer by similarity: feature vectors give the ranking, metadata gives the filter, and both are needed.
Hypermedia adds structure to media through typed links, and messaging must carry the link plus its timing information.
QoS is only useful when it is measured as numbers: bandwidth, delay, jitter and loss, each with a target.
Streaming works by trading start-up delay for smoothness: segments, client buffer and an adaptive choice of bitrate.
An operating system serving continuous media must schedule against deadlines; fairness to all tasks is the wrong goal.
Phones and cameras produce media faster than people can watch, so detection, description and indexing must be automated.
Security rests on two different tools: marks that survive processing (watermark, fingerprint) and hashes that change on any edit.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually design-and-justify questions: draw the layered pipeline, then argue one mechanism (buffering, shaping, admission control, scheduling, indexing) against a stated QoS target.

bank.q: Distinguish non-temporal media from temporal media with two examples each, and explain why the distinction changes the design of the storage, transport and presentation stages.
outline: Definition of temporal media: presentation time is part of the meaning
Non-temporal: text, image; order is chosen by user or document
Temporal: audio, video, animation; late data is useless data
Consequence: buffers, timestamps, synchronisation, QoS
Consequence: non-temporal media can be cached and fetched lazily
Example of failure: audio played without timing becomes noise

bank.q: Draw the layered architecture of a multimedia system from capture to presentation and state the job of each layer, naming the interface between two adjacent layers.
outline: Layers: capture → compress → buffer/synchronise → store → deliver → present
Capture: sampling and digitisation, ADC
Compress: encoder and rate control
Synchronise: timestamps, intra-stream and inter-stream
Store: file system, block layout for continuous media
Deliver: transport protocols with timing support
Present: decoder, playout buffer, display clock
Interfaces carry coded units plus timing information

bank.q: Define QoS for a multimedia flow and explain its four measurable parameters with units, giving a typical target value for interactive voice.
outline: QoS as a contract, negotiated and measurable
Bandwidth in kbit/s or Mbit/s
Delay (latency) in ms, one-way and round-trip
Jitter in ms, variation of delay
Loss as a percentage of packets
Voice targets: about 64 kbit/s, one-way delay below 150 ms, jitter below 30 ms, loss below 1%
Why each parameter needs a measurable target to be enforceable

bank.q: Explain hypermedia nodes, anchors and links, and describe how a messaging protocol such as RTP carries link targets and timing between two systems.
outline: Node: a media object, possibly temporal
Anchor: a region or time interval inside a node
Link: typed connection from anchor to target node or position
Link types: navigation, annotation, synchronisation
Messaging: payload plus header with timestamp, sequence number, payload type
Timestamps map media time to a shared clock
Receiver rebuilds the link's timing from the header
Difference from a plain web link: timing is part of the link

bank.q: Design a layered architecture for a video-on-demand service that must start playout within 5 seconds for 50,000 simultaneous users. Justify your choices of segmentation, buffering, storage placement and delivery, and state the QoS target for each.
outline: Pipeline drawn: ingest, encode ladder, segment, store, deliver, client buffer, playout
Segment length 2–10 s and multiple bitrate versions
Start-up: fetch first two segments at low bitrate to hit 5 s
Client buffer target in seconds, not bytes
Storage: replicated media servers or CDN edge near users
Delivery over HTTP with adaptive selection, not one fixed rate
QoS stated numerically for start delay, rebuffering, jitter
Admission or capacity planning to protect targets at peak

bank.q: A client receives video over a link whose available bandwidth swings between 1 Mbit/s and 8 Mbit/s. Describe how adaptive bitrate selection and buffer thresholds keep playout continuous, and what happens when the buffer drains.
outline: Encode ladder of bitrate versions of the same content
Client estimates throughput from past segment downloads
Rule: choose highest version whose bitrate is safely below estimate
Buffer low → step down one or more levels; buffer high → step up cautiously
Buffer measured in seconds of playout, with low and high watermarks
Buffer empty → rebuffer event, playout pauses
Avoid oscillation by hysteresis and by ignoring one-off samples
Report quality as start delay, rebuffer ratio, average bitrate

bank.q: A receiver logs packet sequence numbers and arrival times for an audio stream. Explain step by step how you would compute the playout delay that keeps late loss acceptably low, and how the delay adapts when jitter rises.
outline: Convert arrival times to arrival in media time using timestamps
Delay_i = arrival_i − timestamp_i for each packet
Playout delay estimate from a running average plus a multiple of deviation
Add safety margin; larger margin means more latency
Too small a delay → packets arrive after playout → discarded
Too large → talker overlap, unusable for conversation
Adaptive scheme raises delay slowly, lowers it cautiously
Report resulting late-loss percentage as the QoS measure

bank.q: Design a content-based image retrieval system for a digital library of one lakh scanned images and photographs. Specify the metadata schema, the feature vectors, the index, and the path taken by a query.
outline: Metadata: title, author, date, subject, rights, file format
Feature vectors: colour histogram, texture, shape, optionally learned embedding
Normalisation of vector components before distance
Distance metric: Euclidean or cosine; ranking by distance
Index structure for fast nearest-neighbour search over many vectors
Query path: extract query features → filter by metadata → rank by distance → return top-k with scores
Evaluation by precision and recall on a labelled sample
Human feedback to refine, since similarity is subjective

bank.q: An audio thread must decode one 10 ms block every 20 ms and a video thread one frame every 40 ms. Show how an earliest-deadline-first scheduler would run them and give the utilisation test used to admit the workload.
outline: Periodic tasks with computation time and period
Audio: period 20 ms, deadline 20 ms; video: period 40 ms
Utilisation U = Σ (computation time / period)
Admission test: U ≤ 1 for EDF on one processor
Scheduler picks the runnable task with the nearest deadline
Missed deadline → dropped block or frame, never delayed playout
Priority inversion and blocking under locks must be bounded
Compare with rate-monotonic bound for fixed priorities

bank.q: Compare three delivery architectures for distributed multimedia — a single centralised media server, a content delivery network, and a cloud media service — on latency, scalability, cost and control. Recommend one for a small Indian edtech startup launching live classes.
outline: Centralised: simplest, one timeline, but long paths and a single bottleneck
CDN: edge copies cut latency and origin load, paid per byte
Cloud: elastic encoding and storage, per-minute billing, regional variation
Latency: propagation delay dominates; edge placement matters
Scalability: replication versus origin capacity
Cost model compared in rupees per stream-hour
Consistency of the shared timeline across replicas
Recommendation argued from audience size and budget, with QoS targets

bank.q: Surveillance footage must be proved authentic in a court case. Evaluate a robust watermark, a perceptual fingerprint and a cryptographic hash or signature as evidence, explaining what each survives and what each cannot prove.
outline: Hash or signature: changes on any single-bit edit, proves integrity, fails after legitimate re-encoding
Watermark: survives compression and re-recording, proves origin, but is invisible and may be removed by an attacker
Fingerprint: identifies the same content under edits, useful for matching copies, not for proving who made them
LSB steganography: invisible but destroyed by any processing, so unsuitable as evidence
Chain of custody and logging alongside the technical mark
Limits: no technique proves the camera was not moved
Combination: signature for integrity, watermark for origin, fingerprint for linkage

bank.q: Explain why a general-purpose fair-share scheduler fails continuous media, and evaluate rate-monotonic scheduling against earliest-deadline-first for a mixed workload of audio, video and background jobs.
outline: Fair share gives every task equal time; media tasks need bounded worst-case delay
A late block is discarded, so lateness equals loss
Rate-monotonic: fixed priorities by period, utilisation bound around 69% for many tasks
EDF: dynamic priority, can reach full utilisation, less predictable under overload
Overload behaviour: EDF misses all deadlines together unless guarded
Blocking from shared locks, disk and I/O latency must be bounded
Conclusion: deadlines, admission control and priority inheritance, not fairness

bank.q: A city wants to search thousands of camera feeds and social media uploads for a missing vehicle. Design the analytics pipeline, then evaluate the risks of false matches and of privacy loss, and state the controls you would add.
outline: Pipeline: ingest, decode, detect, describe, index, query, review
Storage tiering: hot recent clips, cold archive
Ontology labels so different sources can be queried alike
Retrieval by feature vector plus metadata filter
False positives: precision and recall measured on labelled data, human review before action
Privacy: purpose limitation, retention limits, access logs
Legal basis and audit trail for searches
Evaluation: does the system save time without generating unusable leads

glossary.def: The integrated presentation of two or more media types, at least one of them temporal, under the control of a single program or document.
Media whose data represents a signal over time, so that correct presentation requires correct spacing between the pieces.
Keeping the samples of one stream evenly spaced at presentation time, which needs a stable playout clock.
Keeping two related streams, such as audio and video, aligned to each other during presentation.
Memory at the receiver that holds arriving media for a short fixed time so that late packets can still be presented in order.
A number in the packet header giving the media time of the first sample carried, used by the receiver to schedule playout.
A machine or cluster whose storage and I/O are arranged to serve many continuous media streams at once.
A set of edge servers that keep copies of media close to users so that latency and origin load are reduced.
Structured description of a media item — title, creator, date, format, subject — stored beside the content and used to filter queries.
A standard for describing multimedia content with metadata and descriptors so that it can be searched and reused across systems.
Retrieval that ranks items by distance between feature vectors instead of requiring an exact match.
Fraction of retrieved items that are relevant; used to judge a retrieval system's accuracy.
Fraction of relevant items that were retrieved; used to judge how completely a retrieval system found them.
A service in which each user chooses what to watch and when, so the server must serve many independent timelines.
A short independently decodable chunk of a media file that a client can fetch and play on its own.
Delivering media continuously so that playback begins before the whole file has arrived.
A task whose correctness depends on finishing before a deadline, not only on producing the right result.
A shaper model in which tokens accumulate at rate r up to depth b, and each packet spends tokens equal to its size.
A signalling protocol that lets a receiver reserve network resources along a path for a flow.
Embedding a mark in the media signal so that ownership or origin can be verified after distribution.
Hiding the existence of a message inside ordinary carrier data, so an observer does not notice a message at all.
A short value computed from the perceived content of an image or clip, nearly equal for near-identical copies and different for different content.
A cryptographic value computed over the exact bytes of a file with a private key, so any later change makes verification fail.
Converting a media file from one codec, bitrate or resolution to another, usually to fit a delivery link or device.
